articles.title: Film lookahead: Twenty highlights to watch out for in 2026
articles.summary: We look ahead to 20 notable films to watch for in 2026, from Oscar hopefuls to potential blockbusters.
articles.body:
The last time we had an epic Christopher Nolan release, in 2023, Oppenheimer - together with Barbie - gave cinema a huge audience boost. Could Nolan's The Odyssey, along with one or two other 2026 releases, produce a similar result?

The industry is hopeful that a number of highly anticipated projects - like Tom Holland's fourth Spider-Man movie, the second Super Mario Brothers film, and The Devil Wears Prada 2 - could lead to a box office bonanza. Not to mention Avengers: Doomsday and the third Dune movie.

Together with Oscar hopefuls like Hamnet, 2026 looks to be a potentially huge year for an industry still feeling the after-effects of the Covid lockdown. Here are 20 films to watch out for in 2026.

Based on Maggie O'Farrell's award-winning book, Hamnet follows the relationship between WIlliam Shakespeare (Paul Mescal) and his wife Agnes (Jessie Buckley), and explores the tragic events that engulf the couple and inspire Shakespeare's play Hamlet.

This fourth instalment of the series that began back in 2002 continues the events of 2025's 28 Years Later. Spike (Alfie Williams) becomes embroiled with a deadly group led by Jimmy Crystal (Jack O'Connell). Meanwhile, Dr Kelson (Ralph Fiennes) enters into a new relationship that could have devastating consequences.

Loosely inspired by the career of British comedian John Bishop, Is This Thing On? is the third film directed by Bradley Cooper, after A Star Is Born and Maestro. It follows a man who unexpectedly tries stand-up comedy and finds he has a talent for making people laugh.

With trailers filled with images representing passion, longing, and suppressed sexual tension , Wuthering Heights is already one of the most talked-about films of 2026. It's directed by Emerald Fennell , whose last film was Saltburn . And once again she's working with Jacob Elordi, who plays Heathcliff. Margot Robbie plays Cathy.

Amanda Seyfried stars as real-life figure Ann Lee, the leader of an 18th Century religious movement known as Shakerism. Originally a Quaker, she moves away from that order and crosses the Atlantic to America, where hundreds join her on her religious journey.

Kevin Williamson, who wrote the original Scream along with two of its sequels, has rejoined the Scream family, this time directing as well as writing the screenplay. In front of the camera, originals Courteney Cox, who played Gale Weathers, and Neve Campbell as Sidney Prescott, also return to face a new Ghostface - who's menacing Prescott's daughter.

Thirty years after the live action Super Mario Bros. movie was a box office failure, an animated take on the adventures of the lively plumber - The Super Mario Bros. Movie - made more than a billion dollars at the box office. This sequel, based on a 2007 game where Mario and Luigi set off to rescue Princess Peach, was inevitable.

Meryl Streep's wry wit as editor of fashion magazine Runway and Anne Hathaway's performance as Andy, the naive newcomer to the fashion world, made the original film a must-watch for millions. Twenty years later both are back . Few details are known right now, but also returning are fan favourites Emily Blunt and Stanley Tucci as Emily and Nigel.

Over three series, The Mandalorian has become the most successful Star Wars TV spin-off. Now its makers will be hoping its popularity can help reinvigorate Star Wars on the big screen, with the franchise's first movie since 2019's Star Wars episode IX The Rise of Skywalker. The film will also star Sigourney Weaver.

This latest Steven Spielberg project is shrouded in secrecy. Even its two-minute teaser trailer doesn't shed much light on the plot. But it does hint strongly at extraterrestrial visitors being revealed to humankind, with a tagline: "If you found out we weren't alone, if someone showed you, proved it to you, would that frighten you?"

The 2020s haven't been an easy time for Pixar. By its own super-high standards, several films have underperformed including Turning Red , Elio and the Toy Story spin-off Lightyear . So they'll be hoping this fifth instalment of its most successful series , and the return of Tom Hanks as Woody and Tim Allen as Buzz can help restore things.

Milly Alcock's brief introduction as Supergirl in Superman was one of the film's highlights. In her own movie, the plot may be about "an epic, interstellar journey of vengeance and justice". But it looks to be equally about her personality - the trailer shows her doing everything from battling bad guys to dancing beneath a glitterball.

The first animated Moana was a huge hit, its sequel Moana 2 an even bigger one, grossing more than $1bn at the box office. So hopes are high for this live-action remake of the original movie, which tells the story of young Moana leaving her island home on a voyage that she hopes can save her people.

Oscar-winning director Sir Christopher Nolan doesn't usually like audiences knowing too much about the plot of his films in advance. In this case, though, his follow-up to 2023's Oscar-winning Oppenheimer is based on Homer's Greek epic, which follows Odysseus (Matt Damon) journeying home after the Trojan War.

At the end of the previous film Spider-Man: No Way Home , a spell cast by Dr Strange caused the whole world - including Peter Parker's girlfriend MJ - to forget that Parker (Tom Holland) was Spider-Man, or that Parker even existed. So many expect the film to explore how he deals with this lonely phase of being a superhero.

16. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Set a quarter of a century before the first Hunger Games film , Sunrise on the Reaping is the story of Haymitch Abernathy (who went on to mentor Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss) taking part in the 50th Hunger Games. It's been reported that both Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson (Peeta) will make cameo appearances .

It's the fourth in the series that began with Meet The Parents. Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Teri Polo, Blythe Danner and Owen Wilson are all back. But there's a question mark over Dustin Hoffman and Barbara Streisand, who played Stiller's parents in previous films . One confirmed newcomer joining the cast is Ariana Grande.

This is another project currently shrouded in secrecy. So far, only one photo has been released, and confirmed plot details are hard to come by. But we do know that the core cast of Dwayne Johnson, Jack Black, Karen Gillan and Kevin Hart are returning. And that this is being touted as the final Jumanji film.

It's been a quietish time for the once all-conquering Marvel Cinematic Universe. Marvel will be hoping that Avengers: Doomsday will live up to expectations and be a box office juggernaut. This film sees Robert Downey Jr returning , but as villain Doctor Doom. Along with a huge ensemble including members of the X-Men.

The third in director Denis Villeneuve's epic space trilogy will be reportedly based on the second Dune novel, Dune: Messiah. The main cast, including Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya, will be reprising their roles, along with newcomer Robert Pattinson. Villeneuve's next project after this will be the next James Bond film.

articles.title: Diddy injured in prison fight with notorious drug kingpin: Reports
articles.summary: Diddy and a Jamaican drug lord known as "Dudus” had a physical altercation that resulted in a severe head injury, sources say.
articles.body:
Editor's note: A prison representative claims the fight never happened. Read more.

( NewsNation ) — Sean "Diddy" Combs ' head injury that sent him to the hospital from prison stemmed from a fight with a notorious drug lord, TMZ reports .

Sources tell TMZ that Diddy and a Jamaican drug lord known as "Dudus" had a physical altercation that resulted in Diddy sustaining a severe head injury.

TMZ reported Combs was taken from the FCI Fort Dix prison in New Jersey around 1 a.m. Saturday for treatment. People magazine confirmed he was hospitalized.

It was not clear where he was treated, but the music producer was conscious and speaking when he was taken back to the prison before sunrise Saturday.

Diddy's prison release date pushed back amid reported luxury behind bars

Combs' release date from FCI Fort Dix was recently pushed back to March 2, 2028. His previous release date was Jan. 21, 2028.

Combs, who is serving a 50-month prison sentence at the low-security prison, was reportedly put into solitary confinement Oct. 1.

It followed NBC News' report that the rapper was receiving special treatment behind bars, including having men cook and clean for him, make his bed, do his laundry and give him Chinese-style massages .

The rapper was found guilty of two counts of transporting women for prostitution, including his ex-girlfriend Casandra "Cassie" Ventura , in July 2025.

NewsNation's Safia Samee Ali and Patrick Djordjevic contributed to this report.

articles.title: Vinhos brancos de Rías Baixas: por que vale a pena provar essas delícias | G1
articles.standfirst: Região espanhola é famosa pelos maravilhosos brancos de uva Albariño.
articles.summary: Região espanhola é famosa pelos maravilhosos brancos de uva Albariño.
articles.body:
No noroeste da Espanha, na região da Galícia, onde o Oceano Atlântico penetra a terra em longos estuários chamados rías , nasce uma das denominações de origem mais admiradas do país: Rías Baixas.

É a terra do Albariño , um vinho branco que conquistou o mundo pelo frescor, pelos aromas exuberantes e pela afinidade com a cozinha do mar.

A região é chuvosa e temperada, muito diferente da Espanha seca e ensolarada do centro-sul. Para evitar o excesso de umidade e o apodrecimento dos cachos, os viticultores tradicionalmente conduzem as videiras em parras (ou pérgolas), em estruturas altas que mantêm as uvas longe do solo para favorecer a circulação do ar.

Os solos são, em geral, graníticos e arenosos, pobres e bem drenados, o que contribui para a mineralidade e a acidez vibrante dos vinhos . As propriedades são extremamente fragmentadas: muitos pequenos viticultores cultivam parcelas minúsculas.

As uvas brancas Loureiro e Godello são importantes na região de Rías Baixas, enquanto a Mencía é destaque entre as variedades tintas. Porém, a protagonista absoluta, e responsável pela maior parte da produção, é a Albariño.

Seus vinhos apresentam aromas de pêssego, damasco, limão, flores brancas e, muitas vezes, um toque de ervas e sal marinho. Na boca, destacam-se a acidez refrescante e a textura untuosa , com final persistente.

A Albariño é muito cultivada também no norte de Portugal, sobretudo na região de Vinhos Verdes , onde é conhecida como Alvarinho. Apesar da proximidade, os estilos dos dois países são diferentes .

Após a vinificação, muitos produtores optam por um período de estágio em tanques de aço inox para preservar a pureza do fruto e a acidez. Em outros casos, o vinho fermenta ou amadurece em barricas de carvalho, podendo passar também um tempo sur lie , uma técnica que acrescenta complexidade à bebida.

A combinação clássica é com frutos do mar: ostras, mexilhões, vieiras, camarões, lagosta e o famoso polvo à galega. O vinho também acompanha peixes grelhados, ceviches, sushi e queijos frescos. Sua acidez corta a gordura e realça a delicadeza dos sabores marinhos. O ideal é servir geladinho, entre 8 °C e 10 °C.

Uma das linhas de Albariño de alta qualidade e melhor custo-benefício produzidas na Rías Baixas é a Chan de Rosas, do renomado enólogo Oscar Montaña. As uvas são cultivadas no Vale del Salnés, berço e coração da produção do vinho Albariño na Galícia.

É a sub-região mais antiga, fria e representativa da Denominação de Origem (D.O.) Rías Baixas, e concentra mais de 60% da produção de uva de toda a região.

Conheça as duas versões de Chan de Rosas que estão disponíveis no Brasil.

Chan de Rosas Albariño Clásico D.O. Rías Baixas

Chan de Rosas Albariño Clásico D.O. Rías Baixas. — Foto: Porto a Porto/Divulgação.

Esse vinho branco apresenta aromas frutados e florais. Em boca, é complexo e com deliciosa untuosidade. Excelente sozinho ou para acompanhar pratos à base de frutos do mar.

Chan de Rosas Albariño Cuvée Especial D.O. Rías Baixas

Chan de Rosas Albariño Cuvée Especial D.O. Rías Baixas. — Foto: Porto a Porto/Divulgação.

Essa versão amadureceu em barris de carvalho francês por 6 meses, período em que todo o vinho passa por bâtonnage semanal, técnica em que a bebida fica em contato com as borras que são mexidas periodicamente para dar mais corpo e sabor.

Apresenta complexos aromas de frutas e flores brancas, com notas cítricas e de maçã. Em boca, destacam-se a mineralidade , o frescor, a untuosidade e a persistência.

Excelente sozinho, também acompanha aperitivos e queijos moles.

articles.title: Professor shares 'most important thing to do' when someone is grieving
articles.summary: Dr Lesel Dawson, co-director of Good Grief Weston, says avoiding grief is not a good way to cope.
articles.body:
Knowing what to say or how to support someone after a bereavement can be difficult. Fear of saying the wrong thing or intruding at a sensitive time can leave people worried about getting it wrong and avoiding reaching out altogether.

But Dr Lesel Dawson, from the University of Bristol, said this is the worst thing people can do.

Speaking ahead of an annual Good Grief Festival that Dawson is co-director of, she said: "The most important thing when helping someone dealing with grief isn't what you say, but that you don't turn away.

"A simple acknowledgement like 'I'm so sorry and I'm here' can mean a great deal, and it's vital to let the grieving person lead - to follow their pace, their language and their need to talk about the person who died."

The associate professor in Literature and Culture also said people avoiding dealing with their own grief can create lifelong challenges.

Improv community 'devastated' by theatre closure

Mum faces heart transplant wait far from home

Dawson's own understanding of grief was shaped by the stillbirth of her younger sister when she was eight years old and learning that for many years her mother blamed herself for the child's death.

"The way we avoid grief can be really harmful to us," Dawson said. "Being able to turn toward the pain of the experience is the only way we process what's happened."

She said the lack of conversation about grief meant it took "a while" to fully grasp what had happened.

Research commissioned by Marie Curie found that while 70% of people feel comfortable talking about death, far fewer have actually had those conversations with family, friends or healthcare professionals.

While her mother struggled to cope with the bereavement, Dawson found an interest in psychology and emotions.

But after Dawson's first son was born at 29 weeks and suffered complications linked to the premature birth, the loss of her sister and the memory of her mother's "great pain" came to the forefront of her mind.

When Dawson revisited the difficult topic of conversation with her mother after her own pregnancy experience, she realised that her mother "felt [the stillbirth] was her fault".

"I said to her, 'was it my fault that my son was born early?' and she said, 'no of course not'.

"I said, 'okay, why can you not show the same compassion to yourself and your own loss?'" Dawson told BBC Radio Bristol.

She added that feelings of blame and guilt were "very common" during bereavement and could lead to "destructive" coping mechanisms.

"The biggest myth about grief is that it happens in neat, orderly stages and that you eventually get over it," said Dawson.

"In reality, grief is messy, unpredictable and deeply individual. People move back and forth between feelings, and the idea of a tidy, linear process simply doesn't reflect how grief actually works."

Following her own experiences with grief, Dawson took up the role of co-director of Good Grief, a festival in Weston-super-Mare that aims to start and normalise conversations about death, dying and bereavement.

The festival, which begins later, offers a number of workshops, music events, talks and light installations until Sunday.

"Grief involves lots of emotions, it involves sadness, but also anger, numbness, jealousy, rage… they're not sequential.

"Everybody's individual. We have our own ways of grieving and coping and we have our own timelines," Dawson said.

If you or someone you know has been affected by the details raised in this story, advice on where to find help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Why Kaley Cuoco and Tom Pelphrey Chose the Unique Name Philomena for Their Baby Girl: ‘Perfect Choice’ (Exclusive Source)
articles.summary: The couple are also parents to 3-year-old daughter Matilda
articles.body:
According to an exclusive source, Kaley Cuoco and Tom Pelphrey were intentional when it came to naming their baby girl Philomena

The couple announced the arrival of their little one on Wednesday, Oct. 14

The insider says that the couple specifically picked their daughter's middle names to honor different family members

Kaley Cuoco and fiancé Tom Pelphrey were intentional about their baby girl's name, Philomena Carmine Bobby Pelphrey.

According to an exclusive source, the new parents, who announced the arrival of their little one on Wednesday, Oct. 14, specifically picked their daughter's middle names to honor different family members.

"They always choose the middle name to honor family members," the insider explains, noting that both of Philomena's middle names are a special nod to the family. "Carmine is a nod to her father, [and Bobby is] a nod to Tom's side of the family."

"They love classic, vintage names, so Philo was the perfect choice for them," the source adds.

The source goes on to share an update on how the newly minted family of four is doing since their bundle of joy joined the family.

"Matilda is so excited to be a big sister," they say. "Everyone is happy and healthy, and they are all loving up on the new addition to their family."

The Based on a True Story star and her fiancé shared the happy news of their daughter's birth on Instagram alongside intimate photos from the hospital.

"🎀Philomena Carmine Bobby Pelphrey🎀. 💖10/12/26💖," Cuoco wrote in her caption. "There are no words to describe this feeling once again. What a blessing."

"We are so grateful for the crazy wild up and down journey that brought us to our little Philo!" continued the proud mom. "Family officially complete 😭Time to bring Matilda's baby home! 😂💕 @tommypelphrey life exploded the minute we met, and the gifts keep coming. I love you forever , girl daddy! 💘."

articles.title: Imran Khan to move to High Court to challenge the notice to leave India by October 28 for participating in CJP protests despite not being an Indian citizen
articles.summary: Actor Imran Khan is preparing to challenge the notice directing him to leave India by October 28, with his legal team expected to approach the Bombay High
articles.body: Actor Imran Khan is preparing to challenge the notice directing him to leave India by October 28, with his legal team expected to approach the Bombay High Court by Friday or Monday. The notice was issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) following allegations that the actor violated the Foreigners Act by participating in a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in Mumbai.Imran, a US citizen and Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, is likely to file the petition through advocate Zulfikar Memon of MZM Legal LLP. According to reports by Bar and Bench, advocates Zulfiquar Memon, Parvez Memon and Chirag Naik will represent the actor.The plea is expected to challenge the legal basis of the notice, arguing that no provision of the law or any rule bars an OCI cardholder from participating in a protest. It has reportedly described the directive asking the 43-year-old actor to leave the country as 'drastic'. Once the petition is filed, his legal team is expected to seek an urgent hearing before a division bench comprising Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna.The controversy stems from a demonstration held at Mumbai’s August Kranti Maidan on October 10, where Imran joined protesters demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The actor was detained by the police during the protest.Following the demonstration, BJP leader Kirit Somaiya filed a complaint alleging that Imran, being a US citizen, had violated the Foreigners Act by participating in a political demonstration. Mumbai Police subsequently forwarded the complaint to the FRRO for necessary action.Acting on the complaint, the immigration authority issued a notice directing Imran to leave India on or before October 28. Reports state that the notice cites his US citizenship and flags his participation in the demonstration as a potential violation of immigration and foreigners regulations.An Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card allows eligible foreign nationals of Indian origin to live in India and access certain long-term privileges. articles.body: Ranbir Kapoor-starrer ‘Ramayana’ is gearing up for a major international push on Thursday, October 15, as Sony Pictures International prepares to roll out the film’s second trailer, weeks before its worldwide release. While the makers have already held promotional events in Los Angeles, the upcoming launch marks the formal beginning of the film’s global campaign by Sony Pictures, which acquired its worldwide distribution rights earlier this year. The sequence shows him confronting Ravana, played by Yash, who strikes the divine elephant and sends it crashing to the ground. “Before me, every head will bow,” Ravana declares in the promo.The TV spot also features a voiceover that sets the stage for the epic battle between good and evil. “In a time when men walked among gods, and evil rose from the darkness — Ravana — humanity had one hope. Not a God, but a man — Rama,” the narration says. Ranbir’s voice, as Rama, is then heard saying, “If I don’t stop him, the world will fall. Titled ‘Ramayana: The Rise of a Legend’ for international audiences, the promo features Rama taking on a gigantic beast in a forest with his arrows.Alongside the international campaign, the makers are preparing for a grand trailer launch in Bengaluru, Yash’s home turf. The upcoming Bengaluru event is expected to bring together Yash, Ranbir, Sai Pallavi, director Nitesh Tiwari and producer Namit Malhotra, along with other members of the cast and crew.Malhotra shared a note on X on Wednesday, explaining the vision behind taking the Indian epic to international audiences.“When we set out to make Ramayana, our dream was always to take one of India’s greatest stories to the world. articles.title: 'Ranabaali’ preview: Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna reunite after their wedding in a period action drama set during the Great Famine of 1876–78
articles.summary: Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna are set to reunite on screen in ‘Ranabaali’, their third film together after ‘Geetha Govindam’ and ‘Dear Comrade’.
articles.body: Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna are set to reunite on screen in ‘Ranabaali’, their third film together after ‘Geetha Govindam’ and ‘Dear Comrade’. Directed by Rahul Sankrityan, the period action drama blends a fictional rebellion against British colonial rule with alternate-history fantasy and mystical elements. Ahead of its theatrical release on October 16, here’s a look at the film’s story, characters, cast and what audiences can expect.‘Ranabaali’ preview: Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna reunite on screenVijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna are reuniting on screen in ‘Ranabaali’, their third collaboration after ‘Geetha Govindam’ (2018) and ‘Dear Comrade’ (2019). The upcoming period action drama marks another chapter in their on-screen partnership, with the actors now also married in real life.Directed by Rahul Sankrityan, the film is set in colonial-era South India and centres on a fictional warrior who challenges British oppression. With its period setting, large-scale action and alternate-history premise, ‘Ranabaali’ aims to combine a story of resistance with elements of fantasy.The film is scheduled to release in theatres on Friday, October 16, 2026, a day after Rajinikanth’s ‘Jailer 2’.A fictional story set during the Great Famine of 1876–78‘Ranabaali’ is a fictional period drama set against the backdrop of the Great Famine of 1876–78, a devastating period in colonial Indian history. Rather than presenting itself as a straightforward historical account, the film reimagines the era through an alternate-history narrative.Vijay Deverakonda plays Singanamala Bobbili Ranabaali, a rebellious warrior from Rayalaseema who rises against British colonial forces to protect his people. The actor appears in an intense, rugged avatar, with the character positioned at the centre of the film’s conflict.Rashmika Mandanna plays Jayamma, Ranabaali’s wife and partner in his struggle. Her character is closely connected to the protagonist’s personal life as well as the larger fight against colonial oppression.The film’s premise draws on a historical setting while using fictional characters and events to explore what might have happened if history had unfolded differently.‘Ranabaali’ blends alternate history with mystical and fantastical elementsAlthough rooted in a colonial-era setting, ‘Ranabaali’ also incorporates fantasy and alternate-history elements. Director Rahul Sankrityan, known for films such as ‘Taxiwaala’ and ‘Shyam Singha Roy’, has described the project as an imaginative response to historical events rather than a literal retelling of the past.Speaking to Gulte Pro, Rahul explained the thinking behind the film’s alternate-history approach.“Ranabaali is pure fantasy to me, born out of anger. Nowadays, people call it alternate history. The film talks about how it’d look if things happened differently. How would it be? When you hear that kind of history, you feel like, if I were there or had a chance, I’d do things differently. There’s this sort of urge or anger. That anger gives rise to fantasy,” he said.The approach allows the filmmaker to imagine a different course of events within a recognisable historical setting. The film also marks Vijay’s reunion with Rahul after their earlier collaboration on ‘Taxiwaala’.Hollywood actor Arnold Vosloo plays the antagonist‘Ranabaali’ features South African actor Arnold Vosloo, best known internationally for playing Imhotep in ‘The Mummy’ franchise, as its antagonist. Vosloo plays Sir Theodore Hector, a fictional character inspired by British colonial administrator Sir Richard Temple, who was associated with the administration’s response to the Great Famine of 1876–78. The character forms a key part of the film’s conflict with Ranabaali and the people he seeks to protect.The cast also includes Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna in the lead roles, with the story combining their characters’ personal relationship with a larger confrontation against colonial power.‘Ranabaali’ censor details and release date‘Ranabaali’ has completed its censor formalities and received a U/A certificate from the Central Board of Film Certification, according to reports published ahead of its release. The film was originally scheduled to arrive in theatres on September 11, 2026, before being postponed. It is now set for a worldwide theatrical release on Friday, October 16. The film’s listed runtime is approximately 2 hours and 58 minutes, according to BookMyShow.Its release places it in direct calendar competition with Rajinikanth’s ‘Jailer 2’, which is scheduled to arrive in theatres a day earlier.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: In 1982, Paul Newman started a food brand from his barn kitchen with one condition: the company has donated around USD 600 million in profits to charity
articles.summary: Discover how Paul Newman transformed a simple salad dressing into a philanthropic powerhouse, donating over $600 million to charity through his food brand. Learn about his legacy and charitable initiatives.
articles.body: The story of how Paul Newman's kitchen and salad dressing transformed from a playful kitchen batch into a USD 600M+ philanthropic empire is one of the most remarkable social enterprise models in business history. The project originally started when Paul Newman and his friend, author A.E. Hotchner, started making homemade oil-and-vinegar salad dressing in Newman's barn.Rather than profiting from it, they bottled it in old wine bottles and gave it as Christmas gifts to neighbors and friends. However, when family and friends kept coming back for refills, Hotchner suggested they profit from it and start selling recipes in stores. Newman was initially hesitant about putting his name and face on a commercial product, but he agreed under one strict condition: all profits after taxes would go to charity.In 1982, Paul Newman started his own food brandIn 1982, Paul Newman agreed to launch his own food brand consisting of homemade oil-and-vinegar salad dressings, among other things. The Associated Press reported at the time that the duo launched only one product initially and expected the brand to fail soon after its market launch. However, the company instead generated over USD 300,000 in profit in its first year alone. Newman famously remarked during one of his press features at the time, "The embarrassing thing is that the salad dressing is outgrossing my films."Paul Newman and his family expanded on the businessAfter a while, the team behind the brand started seeing massive profits, which led them to venture out with pasta sauces, salsa, popcorn, lemonade, frozen pizza, and pet food, to name a few. Along with this, in 1993, Newman's daughter, Nell Newman, also co-founded another branch under the brand specifically for organic snacks.Paul Newman turned his profits over to the charityAccording to his wishes, the firm's profits continued to be donated to people in need and charity. As one of the initiative launches, Newman founded The Hole in the Wall Gang Camp in Connecticut, a free camp tailored specifically for children suffering from cancer and other serious medical illnesses. This expanded into the global network, which has served over 1.7 million children and families worldwide.Since Newman’s passing, his legacy and charitable efforts have continued and are regularly monitored. articles.title: Saif Ali Khan leases two commercial units in Mumbai for Rs 22.76 lakh monthly rent on a five-year deal, with a security deposit set at Rs 2.36 crore: Report
articles.summary: Saif Ali Khan has given two commercial units in Mumbai on lease for a monthly rent of Rs 22.76 lakh, as per property registration documents.
articles.body: Saif Ali Khan has given two commercial units in Mumbai on lease for a monthly rent of Rs 22.76 lakh, as per property registration documents. The five-year deal covers 5,692 sq ft of RERA carpet area on Andheri Kurla Road.The documents were accessed by CRE Matrix. They show that the actor bought these units only recently, in November 2025.Details of the lease agreementThe leave and licence agreement was registered on September 29, 2026, and runs from May 10, 2026, to May 9, 2031. articles.title: In 1990, Michael Douglas bought a $3.5 million Spanish estate: Inside his 159-year-old Mallorca home with a wine cellar, golf simulator and home cinema
articles.summary: Discover the stunning features of Michael Douglas' Spanish estate, S'Estaca, including its wine cellar, golf simulator, and breathtaking Mediterranean views.
articles.body: For Hollywood star Michael Douglas, luxury is not just about owning a spectacular property. Sometimes, it is about finding a place where the world feels quieter. His sprawling Spanish estate, S’Estaca, offers exactly that, with historic stone buildings, sweeping Mediterranean views and plenty of space to escape the attention that comes with decades in the film industry.Douglas purchased the property in 1990 with his then-wife, Diandra Luker, for a reported $3.5 million. Located near Valldemossa on the island of Mallorca, the 190-acre estate has since become a retreat that he shares with his wife, actress Catherine Zeta-Jones. While its wine cellar, swimming pool and private entertainment spaces make it an impressive celebrity home, its real attraction appears to be the privacy and connection with nature.Michael Douglas’ 159-year-old home overlooks the Mediterranean SeaThe main residence at S’Estaca dates back to 1867, long before Douglas became one of Hollywood’s most recognisable actors. Its history is closely associated with Archduke Ludwig Salvator of Austria, who developed the property after falling in love with Mallorca’s landscape.In a recent interview with The Wall Street Journal, the actor offered a glimpse into the estate and what makes it special to him. He described enjoying the natural surroundings, peaceful views and privacy that the property provides.One particularly personal detail stands out. Douglas has a favourite fuchsia-coloured armchair positioned beside an open window facing the sea. It is an understated feature in a home filled with impressive amenities, but it captures the appeal of the property: a comfortable place to sit, watch the water and enjoy a slower pace of life.The estate’s Mediterranean setting also distinguishes it from a conventional Hollywood mansion. Rather than being defined solely by elaborate interiors, S’Estaca draws much of its character from the surrounding mountains, greenery and coastline.Five apartments, two cottages and space for guestsS’Estaca is not simply one large house. The estate includes five apartments and two cottages, creating several separate living spaces across the grounds. According to Francis York's property profile, the buildings can accommodate up to 20 guests.The layout makes the property suitable for extended family stays and gatherings with friends, while allowing guests to enjoy their own space. Its amenities include a library, games room, gym, heated swimming pool and outdoor kitchen.The estate has also undergone substantial renovation since Douglas acquired it. Francis York reports that the actor spent approximately $7 million on restoration and improvements, modernising the historic buildings while retaining their distinctive character.The result is a blend of old-world architecture and contemporary comfort. The property offers the scale expected of a celebrity retreat without losing the charm of a traditional Mediterranean estate.A wine cellar with a surprising Hollywood twistOne of S’Estaca’s most unusual features is its multifunctional wine cellar. According to the People report, the space contains a TrackMan golf simulator, allowing Douglas to practise his game indoors. It also doubles as a home cinema.The combination makes the cellar more than a traditional storage space. It brings together two very different leisure activities in one private setting, reflecting how the historic estate has been adapted to suit modern tastes.Outside, the property has its own vineyards, vegetable garden, almond trees and olive trees. Francis York’s profile also notes that the vineyard produced locally recognised wine.These features give S’Estaca a distinctly rural atmosphere. Alongside the swimming pool and entertainment facilities, the gardens and cultivated land offer another way to enjoy the property beyond its interiors. The estate is also described as having a spring-water well and a power generator, adding to its independence from conventional services.Why did Michael Douglas once try to sell his Mallorca estate?Despite its appeal, S’Estaca has not always been a permanent fixture in Douglas’ plans. According to Architectural Digest's report on the property, the estate was first listed for sale in 2014 at around $60 million. It subsequently returned to the market at a lower asking price, but the sale did not materialise.The property was taken off the market in 2020, according to Francis York’s account of its listing history. Earlier reports also documented the complicated period when Michael Douglas and Luker shared the estate following their divorce.Today, S’Estaca remains notable for more than its reported purchase price or celebrity ownership. Its 19th-century origins, secluded location and mix of historic charm and modern amenities give it a character that few conventional luxury homes can replicate.What makes Michael Douglas feel special about his Mallorca home which is not just its size or luxury. articles.summary: Data investigation casts doubt on claims that Israeli counter-documentary to ‘NAZA’ received 40 million views.
articles.body:
An Al Jazeera investigation has exposed holes in claims that an Israeli counter-film to the acclaimed documentary NAZA achieved more than 44 million views. By examining domain registries, web archives, source code, and three independent traffic tools, the investigation exposed the fabricated numbers adopted by official Israeli entities to promote the film.

The original award-winning film, NAZA, draws on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers, accusing the army of using artificial intelligence-powered targeting systems to kill numerous civilians in Gaza. The documentary takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in air strikes. After winning the special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival and receiving a historic 25-minute standing ovation , the film was scheduled to screen in 56 countries.

The success of the original documentary triggered a political storm in Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded that the chief of general staff, the head of the Shin Bet, and the attorney general launch a comprehensive investigation into the participants and prosecute them for information security violations.

The film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, were accused of treason, and Netanyahu and Culture Minister Miki Zohar threatened to revoke their Israeli citizenship.

To counter the film’s global resonance, opponents created a counter-film. On September 16, just days after NAZA premiered, the domain nazadocumentary.com was registered via Cloudflare, with the owner’s details hidden.

The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine revealed the site initially disguised itself as the official NAZA website, listing the directors’ names and information on screenings and press. However, it described the film as exposing the systems behind the calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza. By September 30, this deceptive page vanished, replaced by a new title, “NAZA: The Real Story”.

The individuals behind the 49-minute counter-film are Ariel Averbuch, Roy Danino, and Hagai Gutman, who claimed the work was self-funded. Later, two more domains, whatisnaza.com and watchnaza.com, were registered to redirect users to the counter-film.

By the morning of October 14, the nazadocumentary.com website’s counter displayed 43,758,421 views, without disclosing the source of the number or how it was calculated.

Public platforms told a drastically different story. The full 49-minute version of the film on its official YouTube channel had not exceeded 130,000 views by the same date. This means the website’s counter displayed roughly 336 times the actual viewership. The YouTube channel had fewer than 2,000 subscribers, and the film’s account on X had only 170 followers.

Independent traffic analysis platforms confirmed the discrepancy. The US-based platform Semrush estimated the site’s total visits by October 8 at about half a million. Israeli-founded Similarweb estimated only 326 visits for September. Furthermore, the film’s domains were absent from the Tranco list of the world’s top one million visited domains.

An examination of the page’s source code revealed that the element displaying the huge number was internally tagged as “visitors” but displayed to users as “views”. The number is delivered directly from the site’s server, making its calculation method invisible from the outside. Upon opening the page, the counter begins at 97 percent of its value and counts up for three seconds, creating the illusion of a live counter.

Additionally, the site collects actual viewing data without publishing it, sending a “watch-tracker” file after about 25 seconds of video playback to identify the viewing session and parts watched, leaving it unknown whether the counter is based on this data.

Despite the seemingly fabricated metrics, official Israeli accounts spearheaded the promotion of the counter-film. The Israeli Embassy in Washington promoted it on October 3 on social media.

Tzipi Hotovely, head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate, awarded the three creators certificates of recognition for countering the original film. Hotovely said the film had garnered tens of millions of views, transforming an unsupported, fabricated number into an official talking point.

This elaborate digital campaign unfolds against the backdrop of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023. Since the conflict started, Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

articles.title: Some great games to play before GTA VI and Zelda launch
articles.summary: Ahead of the launch of GTA6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, great new titles like Dressmaker and Castlevania can help fill in the gap.
articles.body: You could say we’re in the eye of the storm right now. The storm, of course, being the fall and winter release calendar for new video games. Things started out with a hectic few weeks that were packed with major titles like Control Resonant, Marvel’s Wolverine, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, and Gears of War: E-Day. Meanwhile, next month will be dedicated almost entirely to two gigantic games: Nintendo’s remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and the long-anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI. But even though things are comparatively quiet at the moment, there are still a handful of great games that have come out recently. Even better: Many of them are short enough that you can easily squeeze them in before your life is taken over by Hyrule and Vice City. Here are eight titles you can check out before things get overwhelming again. [Media: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Available on the PS5, Xbox, Switch, and Steam. This new Castlevania game from the studios that worked on Dead Cells has everything I could have hoped for: intricate levels, challenging platforming, tough bosses, and secrets upon secrets to discover. Sometimes, the game got a little too tough, but thanks to some generous assist settings, I could tweak the experience to be exactly what I wanted it to be. Belmont’s Curse whips.—JP [Media: Dressmaker Available on Steam. South African developer Free Lives — known for decidedly not-cozy games like Broforce and Genital Jousting — has ventured into the “cozy” space with Dressmaker, a game about designing and sewing dresses, via a small internal team dubbed Cozy Lives. From your small village shop, you take commissions, sketch designs, pick fabrics and accessories, cut the dress patterns, pin them on a mannequin, and sew it all together. There is a lot of creative freedom. You could certainly spend dozens of hours meticulously designing and accessorizing your dresses — I definitely have — but you can also play in relaxed half-hour sessions when inspiration strikes, making it a flexible option in a pretty packed season for games.—KP [Media: Heartworm Available on the Xbox, PlayStation, Switch, and PC. Resident Evil and Silent Hill are as big as they’ve ever been, but if you’re looking for that old-school survival horror vibe, Heartworm is the game. It looks and plays like a long-lost PlayStation classic — you even have limited inventory — albeit with some optional concessions for modern players, like getting rid of the dreaded tank controls. It also has an interesting twist as your character carries around a camera that serves as both a flashlight and a weapon, giving the game its own distinct-yet-familiar feel.—AW [Media: Orbitals Available on the Switch 2. As far as co-op puzzle-solving goes, Orbitals doesn’t reinvent the wheel. But it nails the fundamentals, and it does so in a pitch-perfect ’90s anime package that elevates it beyond a stock puzzle adventure. The world and character designs are reminiscent of the peak Toonami days — the timeless art of Akira Toriyama or the stylish sci-fi of Cowboy Bebop — and are gorgeous even if you aren’t particularly nostalgic for the era. It’s short enough to finish in a few sessions, and because Orbitals comes with a “friend pass” that allows someone else to play with you without buying their own copy, it’s easy to get a friend to join you for the journey.—KP [Media: Silver Pines Available on the PS5, Xbox, Switch 2, and PC. This is a game best explained in relation to things that already exist. It has the 2D exploration of Metroid, controls like a point-and-click adventure, the slow-burning survival horror of early Silent Hill and Resident Evil, and a weirdo Americana vibe that’s clearly inspired by Twin Peaks. That may sound derivative, but Silver Pines is unlike anything I’ve ever played, a detective story that’s a mix of straight-up terror and deliberate and methodical exploration. It even makes you spend (fictional) money to save your game and you can relax with a cup of coffee to increase your stamina.—AW [Media: Toem 2 Available on the PS5, Xbox, and Switch. Toem 2 is a sequel to 2021’s black-and-white indie game about photography, and it’s just as lovely as the original. The characters are charming, the quests are silly, and taking pictures is a snap. It was a great travel companion during a recent trip, especially because I was able to finish it over the course of a couple hours.—JP [Media: Toy Story: Retro Roundup Available on the PS5, Xbox, Switch, and Steam. For those interested in video game history, any game with the Digital Eclipse name on it is worth checking out. Even still, a Toy Story collection doesn’t seem as immediately interesting as, say, a history of Karateka or Tetris. But through some fascinating archival material coupled with the actual games, the collection makes it clear how technically ambitious these games were, from squeezing 3D sprites on the Sega Genesis to a surprisingly open-ended A Bug’s Life adventure. Just as important, they’re still fun to play.—AW [Media: Well Dweller Available on the PS5, Xbox, Switch, and PC. In Well Dweller, an indie Metroidvania from developer Kyle Thompson, you play as an adorable bird in a world filled with cute characters and alarmingly grotesque bosses. The zones are weird and memorable, like a docks level where you jump from dead fish hanging in nets, but they’re a blast to explore, especially because Glimmer’s matchstick weapon cleverly serves double duty as a springboard you can stick to walls. Well Dweller came out of nowhere for me, and it’s easily become one of my favorites of the year.—JP

articles.title: Madonna felicita a su hija Lourdes con un desgarrador relato sobre su nacimiento: “Fue dramático, como nuestras vidas”
articles.standfirst: La ‘Reina del Pop’ ha compartido un profundo mensaje en sus redes sociales
articles.summary: La ‘Reina del Pop’ ha compartido un profundo mensaje en sus redes sociales
articles.body: La cantante Madonna ha felicitado públicamente a su hija mayor, Lourdes Leon, compartiendo los dramáticos y angustiosos detalles que rodearon su nacimiento hace justo 30 años. La ‘Reina del Pop’ recordó las complicaciones médicas del parto y el abrumador circo mediático que montaron los medios de comunicación en el exterior del centro médico de Los Ángeles. A través de sus redes sociales oficiales, la artista rememoró aquel 14 de octubre de 1996 definiendo la llegada al mundo de su primogénita como un momento sumamente "dramático", pero reafirmando la profunda conexión "bíblica" y las "dos caras de la misma moneda" que comparten ambas en la actualidad. “¡Feliz cumpleaños, mi Lolita! Llegaste a mí en un sueño. Un sueño febril. Un sueño llamado vida. Si intentara escribirlo todo, lloraría un mar de lágrimas”, comenzaba diciendo Madonna en un profundo mensaje publicado en su perfil de Instagram. “Después de 18 horas de parto y el latido de tu corazón disminuyendo, una cesárea de emergencia era la única opción”, confesaba, adjuntando varias imágenes de las dos juntas. “¿Mencioné los helicópteros y los equipos de noticias sobrevolando nuestras cabezas en el último piso del hospital en el este de Los Ángeles? Tu nacimiento fue dramático. Como nuestras vidas. Nuestra conexión es bíblica. Cuando le pido a Dios que me lo explique, Él me dice: ‘¡Mírate al espejo!’. Somos dos caras de la misma moneda”, proseguía Madonna, sobre esa parte incómoda de la fama. Finalmente, la superestrella estadounidense dejaba una bonita reflexión: “Si lo que arriesgamos revela lo que valoramos, entonces lo arriesgaría todo por ti. Nunca olvides quién eres, estrellita, brillando más que todas las estrellas del cielo. Nunca olvides cómo soñar, mariposa. Nunca olvides de dónde vienes. Con amor”, sentenciaba.

articles.title: Mahesh Tinaikar passes away: Farhan Akhtar, Vishal Dadlani pay tribute to Indian rock legend
articles.summary: Farhan Akhtar has paid an emotional tribute to veteran rock guitarist Mahesh Tinaikar, who has passed away at the age of 63.
articles.body: Farhan Akhtar has paid an emotional tribute to veteran rock guitarist Mahesh Tinaikar, who has passed away at the age of 63. The late guitarist was a founding member of the pioneering band Rock Machine, which later became known as Indus Creed. Let's take a look at the 'Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara' actor's tribute.Farhan Akhtar’s tribute to Mahesh TinaikarAccording to the ANI report, Mahesh Tinaikar died of a heart attack. Farhan Akhtar posted a black-and-white photo of the guitarist performing on stage on his Instagram story. He added a short but heartfelt message: "RIP brother #maheshtinaikar," he wrote.Vishal Dadlani remembers the guitaristThe news has led to an outpouring of grief in India’s music community, with musicians, artists and fans remembering his role in the country’s independent rock scene.Singer and composer Vishal Dadlani also mourned the loss and spoke about the lasting influence Tinaikar had on generations of rock musicians. “I feel like I’ve been kicked hard in the chest,” Dadlani wrote in his tribute.He said that every rock-and-roller in India since the days of 'Rock Machine' owed Mahesh Tinaikar a deep debt of gratitude. According to Dadlani, the guitarist had lit a path that once seemed impossible to imagine.Vishal Dadlani also offered condolences to Mahesh Tinaikar’s family, fans and fellow musicians, including Uday Benegal, Mark Selwyn, Zubin Balaporia, Shantanu Hudlikar and Farhad Wadia.Role in Indian rock musicTinaikar was a founding member and lead guitarist of Rock Machine, and he helped shape an important chapter in the story of Indian rock. The band was formed in 1984 and later took the name Indus Creed. articles.title: Why Did Pablo Torre Want to Investigate Kelly Clarkson’s Birdgate? “This Had the Making of a Modern Morality Play”
articles.summary: The sports and culture journalist talks to THR about how he approaches his investigations while also embracing what people are talking about online.
articles.body:
Who would have thought a battle between a pop star/talk show host and a Brooklyn magic shop would dominate the cultural conversation online?

Indeed, Kelly Clarkson and her Very Online beef with Art of Play over a $15,000 (or is that $15,000,000 ?) bird automaton has been the story that everyone was talking about this week. But it was Pablo Torre, the host of Pablo Torre Finds Out , who actually advanced it by obtaining the security camera footage of Clarkson's visit to the store, letting viewers see the interaction in question for themselves.

Torre, of course, is the journalist who broke the Los Angeles Clippers-Kawhi Leonard salary cap scandal, an investigation that resulted in the team and owner Steve Ballmer facing steep penalties and a possible criminal investigation. He was also on The Hollywood Reporter's New York power list earlier this year thanks to his work breaking that story. Oh year, he won a Pulitzer for it too.

THR caught up with Torre to find out why, exactly, he wanted to look into the Clarkson spat, what goes into producing his show, and sitting at the intersection of the worlds of journalism and the creator economy. (The interview has been edited for length and clarity.)

First of all, why did you even decide to look into this?

On my show, we do have a tendency to take stupid things seriously, and also sometimes serious things stupidly. But this is a story that I became obsessed with because I live here in New York City. I had been to that shop before. I am actually a big on-the-record Kelly Clarkson fan, and this had the making of a modern morality play, in which everyone was trying to figure out what's true. My show does, I would say, investigations into culture in every investigation that we do into sports, and this felt like something that I think we could contribute to.

I was gonna say one of the things that I love about the show is that you will take months on a really serious deep-dive investigation, but if something's happening in pop culture, you are not afraid to dive in and explore that. How do you balance those? I have to assume you have a lot of investigations happening at any given time, but sometimes stuff happens. What does it take to reach the level where you feel like, okay, I think we can contribute something to this?

Torre: We are learning that in real time. This is all feeling to me as we make the show, like an experiment, and the returns on our many month investigations, our deepest dives, have yielded a level of result that is beyond our imagination.

But the thing we're also doing as people who exist on the internet and in the real world is always trying to figure out: Is this thing that's breaking right now something that we can we can illuminate? And in that way, I don't think there is anything resembling a rule or a standard for when we blow up a given week that we had planned very carefully for months because a fucking bird automaton became the center of a national controversy.

That is a sentence that, if you were to tell that to me a week ago, I would have felt like I was on acid. But maybe there's a breaking news story that makes you feel like you're on drugs, and the only way to sober up is journalism. I'm sort of workshopping this with you now on the phone. Maybe that's the standard for us, but I don't know. And that's kind of the joy is that the unpredictability of what our show ends up being is a mystery box sometimes even to ourselves.

It's interesting because, when you have a real investigation that I'm sure you work on for a long time, it can lead the news cycle. But you're right; sometimes following something that's happening, following the news cycle, if you have a way to contribute, is a way to break through in a way that stands out. We certainly see that. We are just as guilty as everyone else of following the Kelly Clarkson magic shop story.

Well, it's interesting because something I've discovered about my show is that we will do the very deep dives that take sometimes a year, and once they get published and they make an impact on the news cycle, we have seen that the news cycle itself become the best method of our distribution.

We are truly organically benefiting from the fact that we have made news, and I mean that in the sense of the conversation and the coverage, which is organic and not something we can ever control, but then I also mean it in terms of the fact that things happen in real time in response to the story, and also in the unfolding series of events that we're covering. So it becomes a series, and we never know how many parts.

Obviously, with the Clippers story, we're at part 16. In this case, I have no idea if we're ever going to do a sequel on Kelly Clarkson bird stories, but I'm open to it if it's the right approach. But it has all felt like we're stumbling into a pseudo-psychedelic true crime series that we're reporting in real time.

I mean, to be honest, I feel like this is one of those stories that a month from now, 99.9 percent of people will have forgotten about, but in the moment, everyone's obsessed with it, and that's fine. That's part of culture.

So to me, the thing that I grapple with to your very fair point is how do you make disposable things last? And for us, we're always prioritizing stories with durability that have depth and substance. I should point out that the real tipping point for why we wanted to cover this story, in terms of how we did it in our full episode, was we did recognize that there was a depth of conversation around the power of celebrity and how that power can perhaps be abused when it comes to the audience, and that conversation is not just about Kelly Clarkson. That's about Taylor Swift and Beyoncé and Donald Trump and BTS and any super famous person who exists in public for whom their fandom is their business, and what happens when they direct it without explicitly saying the thing, but implicitly it seems like there's a call to action.

At any given moment, how many stories would you say you're in the process of kind of reporting out?

Torre: Oh gosh, our docket is comical. I mean, we have currently right now — I'm looking at our Google Calendar — we have a dozen things in various stages of production. It's hard for me to say because the way that our show works is we are always on some sort of a runway, and we're always unfortunately notifying the people who've been passed with, "Hey, can you focus on this story?" "Can you fit inside of this plane?" "We're gonna get ready for you guys to take off on Tuesday." Sometimes you end up waiting on the tarmac, and so there are some planes — and I'm not kidding — there are two planes right now that I think are A-plus stories that just have zero news peg, and so we've been having these poor people wait on the tarmac for a year, and I so look forward to getting to tell people those stories.

But stuff like this keeps on happening, whether it's the bird automaton or the next huge Ballmer lawsuit or the next sports gambling development in the Eastern District of New York, it's all quite a lot.

To what extent would you say your investigations play out in public versus working behind the scenes? With the Clippers investigation, as you said, it's kind of ongoing. There's installments that have come up after those first couple episodes, but then you talked earlier this week about Fanatics and LeBron James and that relationship.

That's a public conversation that maybe turns into something down the line. Is there a benefit to speaking about this stuff publicly? or is it easier to operate privately and then show it when you think it's ready?

It's a great question, and we talk about this specific question a lot. In general, I would say that we are always doing more than we can share in public, and that's the nature of research. That's the nature of — we're going to make so many calls and follow so many trails into so many weird rabbit holes — and some of those are dead ends.

But sometimes those end up being the signposts that we follow to the actual truth, and so there is a great inefficiency here, just in terms of man, we are that duck that is paddling furiously under the surface. Even as you can see us flapping our wings wildly, you know we're still doing a lot more than I think people can ever see. And I don't mean that to dramatize ourselves. I don't mean that to say that's how neurotic we tend to be, but there are also points in any given story when it's time to show your work, and what we show is what we have deemed to be publishable, what's deemed fair for publication, and once that's out there, yeah, we we pride ourselves on telling you this is why we're doing this. This is how we arrived at this. These are the questions that we still have.

And when we pose a question, sometimes we have a sense of what the answer might be, but sometimes we just don't know, and so it brings me into, for instance — I'll just refer to the Clippers thing because it's the most common frame of reference — It'll lead me into debate with Mark Cuban, in which I think I knew more than Mark at the various points that we were debating. There were things that I had not published that I did have a pretty strong sense of, that informed my confidence and my convictions, but I wasn't ready to report that, and I wasn't ready to say that, and so I didn't say it. And when I was ready to report, that's when the public got it.

One of the things that I appreciate is that you sit at this intersection of journalism and the creator economy, and as someone who is a journalist but follows the creator world pretty closely, it's fascinating to me because there are a lot of journalists at traditional news outlets that have the luxury of spending a lot of time to develop an investigation and publish or release the segment when it's ready.

But if you're a creator, you do have to have a regular cadence of stuff. How did you figure out how to do that? I know you have the partnership with The Athletic, which is obviously very helpful, but how do you make sure that you can feed the beast? Whether it's pure journalism or something like when you had [art critic] Jerry Saltz review sports trophies , how do you make sure you feed that while also doing the journalism that I think you've built a reputation for?

So it's a reverse engineering problem, and so very specifically as a person who has looked into the eyes and I've gotten to meet — I guess they're my fellow creators? Although I don't think I'm necessarily quite doing what they do. But I, like you, I'm fascinated by them because I didn't grow up that way, and I also now have a job that requires three episodes a week.

And so, in that reverse engineering of okay, you have three episodes a week, but your goals are different. Your goals are journalistic, they are along the lines of both following your curiosity and making impact. So within that framework, what do you do? I remember meeting MrBeast recently. He was on Morning Joe , and I was co-hosting the show that day. He's prolific, but also so tired.

Like, they're all burnt out. I think some of them are superhuman, but a lot of them are just tired. And so, really, the reverse engineering problem is: I have myself, and I think I've been privileged to prioritize what I find energizing. At the same time, when I start to create a docket, what I reverse engineer is "Okay, what is the most important stuff that we want to do? What is the shorthand here? What is the Aspiration-level investigation?" Because we're going to work around that, and so once we sort of place that along our calendar, then we start to backfill, and we're like, okay, so that's going to take the most time, the most resources. What's going to take the second most?

There's a version of our show where we come out six times a year, and we just do like the deepest dives … But then there's stuff happening every week, and then you look at the news cycle, and then you figure out, okay, wait a minute, Jerry Saltz. We're fans of him. We love that guy. We're trying to always figure out ways to do sport differently. What if we have him review statues? What if we have a butter sculpture of myself made? Did that feel like a parody of my ego, or also a way to make fun of it? So I think it's sort of how do we plot in things that are different in concept but aren't as heavy a lift? And once you're along that path, which is like a different genre of show, you have a lot of fun. And that's how we have this whole cast of characters who get pulled in to do weird shit. And it's a bit of a palate cleanser for me, and probably I hope for the audience.

To bring it back to Kelly Clarkson: You did end up buying an automaton for a good cause. It's a silly story, but you were able to squeeze in something that I think would actually bring some good to the world. Can you explain why you decided to do that when you when you chose to cover the story?

So, among the levels of why that story passed the bar for us, I should point out, is the fact that as soon as I saw that there was this other preferred automaton that Kelly Clarkson had no interest in, and she had so little interest in it, as evidenced by the tape we obtained of the security cameras, that she didn't even stick around to hear how much it costs, which was $2,000, which is a lot of money.

That occurred to me … Is that too much money for us? Like, if we were to go and buy that other bird, what would we do with it? In that we are I thinking in the spirit of a show like John Oliver's, frankly, where there's a third act, and we've done our own iterations of that.

In the Aspiration Part One episode, we had a guy dressed as Iron Man plant a tree, a sad little apple tree, a sapling, in front of the Intuit Dome. That was our climactic sort of reveal at the very end of that one. This was another little version of that that we've been inspired to do because, in this case, we actually got to bring attention to a real life tragedy. David Samson, who is on these Aspiration episodes with us, who's a friend of the show and is frequently contributing to the show, his daughter Kyra died over the summer, and I had gotten to know her, I've gotten to know David's family, David's now one of my closest friends, and his response to that was the most superhuman thing I've experienced. Which is that he decided to create the Kyra Fund , fighting glioblastoma, searching for a cure, and he proceeded to go back to work. And so, in honor of that, in honor of having a charity and a cause close to home, I thought, what better way to harness the attention to something that feels profoundly stupid, like a truly petty grievance that had saturated all of our brains. How could we turn all of that attention to something positive?

And so we put it up for auction. And my hope is that some incredibly fiscally irresponsible person can realize that they can own a piece of pop culture history and find a cure for one of the worst forms of brain cancer that exists. So, yeah, I hope people take that part seriously as well.

articles.title: Loles León, actriz, contra las trabas en vivienda: "Aquí se tiene que alquilar a todo el mundo, todos necesitamos un techo"

articles.summary: La actriz denuncia las trabas de los propietarios para alquilar a personas mayores
articles.body: La vivienda es un problema transversal que afecta a todos por igual. Algo de lo que está muy concienciada la actriz Loles León que ha relatado en el programa 'A la carta' de la Cadena SER los graves impedimentos que encontró al intentar alquilar un piso en Madrid debido a su edad, una discriminación que la llevó a plantar cara a los propietarios: "Me dijeron que los dueños no alquilan a gente de 70 años y yo, claro, ya tenía 74. Y le dije: 'Ah no, pues es que yo tengo 74'. Me dijo: 'No, pero tú eres diferente'. Digo: 'Yo, ¿diferente por qué?' Dice: 'Pues porque eres tú'. Digo: '¿Eres tú? Pues mira, ¡eres tú! No lo quiero'", sentenció. Indignada por el trato de favor que pretendían ofrecerle solo por ser una figura pública, la actriz rechazó la oferta para denunciar una problemática que afecta a miles de ciudadanos: "No lo alquilé, porque dije: 'Aquí se tiene que alquilar a todo el mundo, todos necesitamos un techo, todos necesitamos una casa para vivir, y encima con los alquileres que estáis metiendo. Pero que a mí me lo alquiláis porque soy una persona conocida, y a lo mejor viene ahora una señora de 74 que también lo necesita, y no se lo alquiláis porque no queréis viejos en las casas, ¡pues iros a tomar por culo!' Y me fui". Finalmente, León logró conseguir un inmueble evitando el trato directo con particulares y recurriendo a la vía corporativa: "Llegó alguien que, pues por empresa. No por propietarios particulares. Las empresas te los alquilan, claro. Tienen pisos y te los alquilan, no les importa la edad que tengas". Sin embargo, la intérprete criticó con dureza las excesivas condiciones financieras y administrativas que imponen en el mercado actual: "Te piden hasta si te han hecho una ecografía, un análisis o una psicología de estas que nos hacen. Te lo piden todo, ¿eh? Y no sé cuánto dinero de que si para dos de fianza, el de la inmobiliaria, el corriente, el depósito no sé qué por si rompo algo... Bueno, todo eso, un dineral que no todo el mundo lo puede tener". Concluyó mostrando su firme respaldo a las movilizaciones sociales por el derecho a un techo digno: "Por eso está tan mal la vivienda, y por eso está la Puerta del Sol como está. Bravo por toda esta gente que está allí, yo lo pongo todo en Instagram. Es que he estado de viaje, por eso no he podido ir".

articles.title: Danny Trejo says he is ‘not pro-ICE’ after being cast in movie from Ben Shapiro’s company
articles.summary: For decades, Hollywood actor Danny Trejo’s bread and butter was playing gangsters, prison inmates and other assorted criminals.
articles.body: For decades, Hollywood actor Danny Trejo’s bread and butter was playing gangsters, prison inmates and other assorted criminals. So when Trejo was offered the chance to a play a hardworking, peace-loving Mexican shop owner in a thriller with a working title of “Pawn Shop,” the 82-year-old actor “jumped at the idea of playing a good guy,” his son, Gilbert Trejo, posted to social media. Now Trejo is catching flack for taking part in what’s been described as a pro-ICE movie that is being produced by conservative media outfit The Daily Wire, which was founded by political commentator Ben Shapiro. “I am a proud Mexican who has always been and will always be a supporter of my community,” Trejo wrote in an Oct. 9 post on Instagram. “I am also obviously pro immigrant. I am not pro ice.” But Trejo gave no indication in the post if he knew who was producing the movie when he signed onto the movie, and closed by declaring “I am an actor. My job is to tell a story.” His son, however, insisted that Trejo did not know Shapiro was involved in the movie until two weeks into the shooting. “My 82-year-old dad has never heard of Ben Shapiro,” he wrote. “I had to explain to him who that is, and what kind of guy he is.” Shapiro did not immediately respond to an NBC News request for comment. Now, Trejo is “handcuffed to this stupid project, and swaths of people have instantly turned their back on him without knowing any of the facts,” Gilbert Trejo said. “My dad contractually can’t bad mouth him, the film, or walk away without being sued for breach of contract,” he added. “He couldn’t even release the statement he wanted to.” “His agent described it as ‘a complicated story about a complicated time, where everyone looks bad except you, the hardworking Mexican shop owner who just wants peace,’” he wrote. Trejo is represented by Gloria Hinojosa, who works for the Los Angeles-based boutique talent agency Amsel, Eisenstadt, Frazier & Hinojosa, Inc. She did not return an email for comment. The movie, which is being shot in Livingston, Montana, also stars Harvey Keitel — another tough-guy actor who is known to be ideologically opposed to Shapiro and his ilk. He is represented by Stephanie Simon of Untitled Entertainment. She, too, did not respond to a request for comment. So it was not clear if either Trejo or Keitel were aware of the synopsis of “Pawn Shop,” which now appears on IMDB, before they signed onto the movie. “When chaos hits the streets of Minneapolis, a young federal agent is left alone after his partner is seriously hurt and must find a way to survive an increasingly dangerous situation. Seeking shelter inside a neighborhood pawn shop, he becomes trapped with a traditional Hispanic father and his progressive college-age son, forcing three very different men to confront fear, conflicting beliefs and a crisis that tests their courage and humanity.” The film set has been the site of numerous protests after behind the scenes video appeared to show the movie will have a sequence based on the January 2026 fatal shooting of Renée Good by an ICE Agent in St. Paul, Minnesota.

articles.body: Veteran actors Raza Murad and Gajendra Chauhan have reacted to the row around actor Imran Khan, who has been asked to leave India by October 28 after joining a protest in Mumbai. Both actors told ANI that a foreign national should not get involved in the country’s internal matters and that the law must be followed.Raza Murad backs the police action against Imran KhanRaza Murad said Mumbai Police was acting within the law and that outsiders have no reason to step into India’s internal matters. He said, "Whether it is Imran Khan or any other foreign national, there is no reason to interfere in the internal affairs of our country. Now I have come to know that Imran Khan has become a US national and he was an actor here. So, as a US national, he has no right to intervene in the internal affairs of our country."He also pointed out that Imran has not been asked to go immediately.“Mumbai Police is doing this in the framework of the law. And he has not been told to leave the country tomorrow or in 24 hours. He has been given 15 days,” the veteran actor said.Raza Murad added that if Imran feels the decision is unfair, he can go to court, and the verdict should be respected whatever the outcome. He said, "If he feels that he is being forced out of the country, then he can approach the court."Gajendra Chauhan says violation should be punishedActor Gajendra Chauhan also reacted strongly. He said Imran Khan, as an American citizen, should not have taken part in the protest. According to him, people living in India on an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card face certain restrictions, and any breach should invite action.He said, "He is an American citizen, and he was living here. I don’t think he should have gone to protest because it is against the law. If someone lives on an OCI card in India, he cannot fight the elections, cannot vote, and cannot protest. So, if he has done it, definitely he should be punished."Gajendra Chauhan also questioned the time given to Imran to leave and suggested that the authorities should act faster. He said he was disappointed that Imran joined the protest despite the fame, money and love he had received in India.He said, "You have been such a big celebrity in India. You have earned a name, earned money, earned a position. Indians used to love you. Despite that, you go to such a protest, which is against the residential values on which you are living in India. It is a violation of the law. And when there is a violation of the law, then the punishment will be there."Why Imran Khan was asked to leave IndiaImran Khan, nephew of Aamir Khan, was given a ‘Leave India’ notice by Mumbai Police, directing him to leave the country by October 28. As per reports, he holds an American passport.He had taken part in a protest at Mumbai’s August Kranti Maidan, which demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. articles.summary: Special Forces' Mauricio Umansky revealed where he and Kyle Richards stand three years after their breakup and addressed speculation about the real reason th...
articles.body:
Mauricio Umansky and Kyle Richards ' bond remains as solid as a diamond.

Over three years after The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills stars announced they were ending their 27-year marriage , Mauricio proved there's still nothing but love between him and his estranged wife.

"Kyle and I are great friends, that's the bottom line," the 56-year-old—who shares daughters Alexia Umansky , 30, Sophia Umansky , 26, and Portia Umansky , 18, with Kyle in addition to stepdaughter Farrah Brittany , 37—told E!'s Hot Goss host Eyal Booker and guest host Caleb McDaniel in an exclusive interview. "Obviously we have not filed yet. But to all of these separations that people go through, do it with dignity."

While Mauricio and Kyle's relationship may no longer be romantic, the reality stars will always consider each other family.

"She and I had a relationship for 30 years," Mauricio noted. "She's my best friend, she's the mother of my kids, we loved each other, we love each other."

Of course, Mauricio acknowledged that going through a breakup in the public eye can have a downside—"It's not fun, everybody asking and wondering"—he hopes their cordial uncoupling can help others become friendly exes too.

"If we can teach anybody anything," the real estate mogul explained, "it's how to do it with elegance and dignity and have respect for each other."

As for continued speculation the former couple might be headed for a reconciliation, Mauricio confirmed he and Kyle are not getting back together—for now, at least.

"We just take it day at a time right now," he told E! before adding with a laugh, "I'm not going to give you any insight that I don't have yet."

The Special Forces: World's Toughest Test contestant does, however, have plenty of insight on what it's like training for season five of Fox's grueling reality competition series.

And while he admitted Kyle was not happy when he and Alexia signed up for the show, the experience they shared in the jungles of Malaysia was worth more than a shopping spree down Rodeo Drive.

"Alexia wanted to go on her own, let's just be clear with that," Mauricio explained. "She's an absolute badass. I'm so proud of her. To have that moment between father and daughter and to share a moment like this, it's so intense and physically challenging, mentally challenging, uncomfortable. But to be there, it's priceless."

Mauricio added, "It was the most incredible experience on the planet."
